title: Pyramids of Meroë (Kushite royal cemeteries)
summary: At Meroë, on the Nile in what is now Sudan, the kings and queens of the Kingdom of Kush were buried under small, steep-sided pyramids of sandstone or brick. The northern cemetery was begun in the later 3rd century BCE. The largest pyramids are no more than about 17.5 m square at the base, far smaller than Egypt's.

uncertainty.note: The Past gives the northern cemetery as founded in the second half of the 3rd century BC by King Amantekha; -275 is the mid-point of that half-century (-299 to -250 is the stated span). The kingdom ended in the 4th century AD, after which the pyramids stand as ruins. End is the present.

phases.description: Pyramids built for around 40 kings, queens and princes in the Northern Cemetery from the second half of the 3rd century BC until the end of the kingdom in the 4th century AD (The Past). Individual pyramid dates are not given in the sources opened.

After the kingdom ended in the 4th century AD the pyramids stood as ruins; UNESCO names wind erosion and desertification as main threats today. The start year is the kingdom's end, not a dated collapse.

materials.material: sandstone blocks (later brick or coursed rubble) over a rubble core, originally lime-plastered

reviewer_note: Shape pyramid. A 'typical' royal pyramid is not given in one measured source: base 17.5 m is the largest (UNESCO nomination) and height 30 m is a magazine figure for the large ones; 17.5 m at 73 degrees gives about 28.6 m, so they agree roughly. Smaller pyramids are much lower. Least sure of that height (secondary source) and of the -275 start (mid-point of a half-century); the 350 end is the kingdom's end and the ruined phase start is bridged.
